Concede, object, propose

1 · Read the explanation.
How people actually change each other’s minds

The three moves. Almost every productive turn in a discussion has the same shape: concede something, object to the rest, propose what should happen instead. Well, you have got a point about the cost, but the timing is what worries me — could we start in April? Drop the concession and you sound like an opponent; drop the proposal and the discussion has nowhere to go.

Conceding is not losing. You have got a point, that is fair, I am all for that, I take your point all buy you the right to the word but. In English this is close to obligatory: an objection with no concession in front of it reads as hostility even when it is not meant that way.

Marking an opinion. As I see it, it seems to me that, personally, I think, I would say that all say the same thing: this is my reading, not a fact. It sounds weaker and it is strategically stronger, because you can move later without having to admit you were wrong.

Balancing. On the other hand and that said put a second consideration beside the first rather than knocking the first down. Use them when you want to complicate the picture, not win.

Closing a part. OK, I can agree with X. What about Y? is what turns a discussion into a decision. Say what is settled out loud, then name the next open question.

Question tags. …, do you not? and …, is it not? hand the turn back and invite agreement. In speech they are usually contracted: don’t you?, isn’t it?

The commonest errors at this level
  • Objecting with no concession: No. The cost is fine.
  • Stating opinions as facts: It is obvious that… in every turn.
  • Agreeing so completely that nothing is decided.
  • I am agree instead of I agree, and I am agree with you.
  • Using on the contrary where English wants on the other hand.

Two things to watch

1 — The concession must be real. You have got a point, but you are completely wrong is worse than no concession at all. Name the part you actually accept.

2 — Agree in English with a verb. I agree, I agree with you, I quite agree. Never I am agree.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Building one turn out of the three moves

The other person has said: We should hire a fifth designer — we are two months behind. You think the problem is the brief, not the number of people.

Step 1 — find the part you can accept. Not the conclusion, but something: you are behind. Say it: Well, you have got a point about the timetable,

Step 2 — object to the part you cannot. One sentence, and about the thing, not the person: but I am not sure a fifth designer would fix it, because the brief keeps changing.

Step 3 — propose something with a date. This is what most people leave out: Could we freeze the brief this week and look at hiring again in April?

The whole turn: Well, you have got a point about the timetable, but I am not sure a fifth designer would fix it, because the brief keeps changing. Could we freeze the brief this week and look at hiring again in April?

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Three moves, in that order

Disagreement in English runs concede → object → propose. Skip the concession and the other person stops listening; skip the proposal and nothing changes.

Concede: Well, you have got a point, but… · That is fair, but… · I am all for fun, but I want to learn something — the last of these concedes the value and limits its application, which is the strongest form of concession in an argument. Balance: Yes, but on the other hand… · That said… — the second is more written and slightly cooler. Object: No, but look… is direct and stays open; I am not sure about that is the mildest real objection English has, and is not agreement.

Claiming less on purpose

As I see it…, It seems to me that…, Personally, I think… mark a statement as an opinion. That is not politeness for its own sake: a claim marked as an opinion is harder to attack, because your opponent must argue with your reasoning rather than simply produce a counter-fact. Compare The cost is the whole question with As I see it, the cost is the whole question.

Two moves keep a discussion moving. Banking: OK, I can agree with that. What about April? — settle a part, then move on. Handing back the turn: a tag question, …, don’t you? · …, isn’t it? The tag reverses the main clause: positive statement → negative tag, negative statement → positive tag, and the auxiliary is the one already in the sentence (You have read it, haven’t you?). With no auxiliary, do appears: She works here, doesn’t she?

Errors to watch: I am agree → I agree · I am not agree with you → I do not agree or I disagree · You are right, isn’t it? → aren’t you? · On the other side… → on the other hand · a bare No, that is wrong ends the conversation rather than the point.

Stage 5 · Speaking & WritingWriting

Writing a summary

A summary is not a shorter version of everything. It is the argument, the two strongest reasons, and what was decided.

The brief

Summarise a discussion in 120–150 words for somebody who was not there: what the question was, where the two sides differed, what was conceded, and what was agreed or left open. No dialogue, no names of everybody who spoke, and nothing you cannot support from what was said.

1 · Hold the discussion first. Make notes as you go.
1The question you are deciding:
2Your position, in one sentence:
3The strongest point on the other side:
4What you conceded, and what you got for it:
5What was agreed, and what was left open:
2 · Take the two roles, then swap.
Useful language
  • Opening: As I see it… · It seems to me that…
  • Conceding: Well, you have got a point about…, but…
  • Balancing: Yes, but on the other hand… · That said…
  • Closing: OK, I can agree with… What about…?
Partner AYou
  • Argue that a job you enjoy beats a salary twice the size.
  • Concede at least twice, naming what you accept.
  • Mark every opinion as an opinion.
  • Propose something concrete before you finish.
Partner BYour teacher
  • Argue that enough money has to come first.
  • Use no, but look at least once, and stay in the discussion.
  • Ask what “enough” means in numbers.
  • Close the settled part out loud before the end.

Work in pairs. Five minutes. Then swap sides and argue the position you have just been attacking.Five minutes with your teacher, then swap sides and argue the other position.

Afterwards: name the one concession that moved the discussion furthest.

3 · Write the summary. 120–150 words.
Include
  • the question, in the first sentence;
  • the two positions, one sentence each, in reported speech;
  • what was conceded on each side;
  • at least four items from stage 2;
  • a final sentence saying what was agreed and what was left open;
  • no dialogue and no direct quotation.

1 · Read the model summary of the recorded discussion.
Model · a summary in 140 words

The discussion turned on which five qualities matter most in a teacher. The first speaker began with patience and kindness, arguing that learning is harder than it looks from the front of a room. The second accepted this but objected that a kind teacher who has no ideas teaches nothing, and pushed for creativity.

Two disagreements followed. The first speaker warned that a lesson can be enjoyable and empty; the second replied that a teacher can also be too nice, and proposed strictness. That was the only point neither would concede: strictness was called old-fashioned, and answered with the claim that motivated students do not waste time.

Four qualities were agreed — motivating, supportive, creative and hard-working — with organisation proposed as the fifth. The list was left one place short.
